```java
            .seekRequest(config.seekRequest))));
```

`ForEach` is a component: the static overload maps once per render; the `Signal<List<T>>` overload reads the signal in its tracked render, so only the rows re-render on change. It adds one Group/`VSTACK` wrapper around the rows.

## `LibraryView` with `ForEach`

```java
@Override
public View body() {
    return VStack.make()
            .modifiers(
                    padding(24),
                    frame(f -> f.width(Commands.Size.FILL).height(Commands.Size.FILL)))
            .children(
                    Text.make("Library").modifiers(
                            fontSize(26), FontWeight.BOLD, accessibilityRole(Roles.HEADER)),
                    Text.make(MusicPlayerView.TRACKS.size() + " songs · "
                            + MusicPlayerView.TRACKS.size() + " albums")
                            .modifiers(foregroundStyle(MusicPlayerView.SECONDARY_FG)),
                    Divider.make().modifiers(padding(p -> p.edges(0, 0, 0, 10))),
                    ScrollView.children(
                            VStack.make().children(
                                    ForEach.of(MusicPlayerView.TRACKS, (track, index) ->
                                            TrackRowView.make(r -> r
                                                    .track(track)
                                                    .index(index)
                                                    .trackIndex(config.trackIndex)
                                                    .position(config.position)
                                                    .playing(config.playing)
                                                    .seekRequest(config.seekRequest))),
                                    Spacer.make())));
}
```

Tree: `VStack > [Text, Text, Divider, ScrollView > VStack > [ForEach(Group) > rows, Spacer]]`.

## Performance-first alternative — `TrackList` component

If you want row-scoped re-rendering **without** the `ForEach` wrapper:

```java
final class TrackList implements View {
    private final Signal<List<Track>> tracks;
    private final WritableSignal<Integer> trackIndex;
    // position / playing / seekRequest ...

    @Override
    public View body() {
        List<Track> list = tracks.get();
        View[] rows = IntStream.range(0, list.size())
                .<View>mapToObj(i -> TrackRowView.make(r -> r
                        .track(list.get(i))
                        .index(i)
                        .trackIndex(trackIndex)
                        /* ... */))
                .toArray(View[]::new);
        return VStack.make().children(rows); // the VStack is the component root
    }
}
```

Usage:

```java
ScrollView.children(
    VStack.make().children(
        new TrackList(config.tracks, config.trackIndex, ...),
        Spacer.make()));
```

Only `TrackList` re-renders on a list change; there is no extra Group node because the `VStack` is its root. For a **static** list, the plain `IntStream` stream in `LibraryView.body()` is even simpler — no component, no signal, no wrapper.

If you want, I can plan `ForEach` with both forms: `ForEach.of(...)` (component, wrapper) and `ForEach.views(...)` (static `List<View>`, no wrapper, paired with a `children(Collection<View>)` overload).
But View.of and ForEach is actaully just to improve cpu performance at the cost of dx right?

Not quite. They’re primarily **DX helpers that create an explicit component boundary**; the CPU benefit is a side effect, and the cost is usually **one wrapper node**, not DX.

| Shape | DX | CPU recompute | Extra node |
|---|---|---|---|
| Bare `if` in a small component | More boilerplate | Narrow (that component) | None |
| `View.of` / `ForEach` component | Best (inline, concise) | Narrow (that slot) | One Group/`VSTACK` |
| Stream in the parent body | Best (no wrapper) | Wide (whole parent) | None |

So:

- **`View.of` is not “CPU at the cost of DX.”** It exists because Java has no `if` expression — it lets a branch be an argument to `.children(...)`. Relative to a bare `if` in a parent body it is slightly more code, but it gives an explicit, narrower boundary. Relative to an anonymous `View` class it is much better DX. Its real cost is the Group node.
- **`ForEach` is list DX sugar** (no `ArrayList`, no index capture). A static `ForEach.views(...)` returning `View[]` is a pure DX win with no wrapper. A component `ForEach` adds a Group but scopes list re-renders; the wrapper is the cost, not DX.
- The genuine tradeoff is **boilerplate vs wrapper nodes vs recompute scope**:
  - Small component + bare control flow → best nodes/CPU, worst DX.
  - `View.of` / `ForEach` → best DX, one extra node, scoped CPU.
  - Stream in parent body → best DX and no wrapper, but parent-wide recompute.
- The per-component model already gives CPU scoping. `View.of`/`ForEach` don’t *add* performance; they make the boundary convenient and visible. If anything, they are DX wins over the old `Conditional.when` and manual loops.

So: choose them for **authoring ergonomics and explicit scoping**, and accept the wrapper node — or use small components/streams when you want zero wrappers and don’t mind the boilerplate or wider recompute.

A generated DSL is verified by proving it **emits the same bytes** as the
reference implementations:

1. Port the golden vectors in [CONFORMANCE.md](./CONFORMANCE.md) into the new

### The three operations

Every concrete view exposes the same three operations — **construction**
(`make`), **modifiers** (`.modifiers`), and **children** (`.children`). In the
Java realization `make(...)` **is the only static of the three**; a later call
overrides an earlier value for the same property.

| Operation | Purpose | Canonical (SwiftUI-shaped) |
|-----------|---------|----------------------------|
| **values** | Configure structural/layout values and a control's bound value | `View(config:)` — labels in the constructor |
| **modifiers** | Apply `ViewModifier` values, innermost-first | `.modifier(_:)` / `.padding(_:)` / … |
| **children** | Supply the content subtree (content-bearing views only) | trailing closure `{ … }` |

The **canonical builder spelling** (the recommended form; per-language spellings
are in [§9.3](#93-language-adaptation-rules)) is:

```
ViewName.make(values)              // values   — a config-builder lambda (Java views)
      .modifiers(modifier, ...)       // modifiers — varargs
      .children(view, ...)            // children  — varargs, content-bearing views only
```

In the Java realization a view's values entry is the static `make(...)` (the
construction factory; empty `make()` for config-less or value-less starts).
`modifiers(...)` is an **instance** operation available on the builder and on any
`View` value (the interface default), so it (and `children(...)`) chain on the
builder in any order:

```
VStack.make(v -> v.spacing(8)).children(a, b).modifiers(m)
VStack.make(v -> v.spacing(8)).modifiers(m).children(a, b)
VStack.make().modifiers(m).children(a, b)
```

The old static `X.modifiers(...)` first-call entry points are **removed** —
`modifiers(...)` is an **instance** operation (interface default for bare `View`
values, covariant override on the builder). Static `X.children(...)` is **kept**
as a value-less first-call convenience (`HStack.children(a, b)` ≡
`HStack.make().children(a, b)`); `make(...)` is the only values static.

**Values are a config-builder lambda.** `make { c in … }` populates a per-view
fluent **config** (`VStack.Config`, `Text.Config`, …). It is the *same type* a
style's `makeBody(Config)` receives ([§5.7](#57-styleable-controls-the-style-contract)).
The builder is **fluent and mutable**: setters return the config. Config-less
views (`Divider`, `Spacer`) take an empty `make()`.

**Every value member is reactive-capable (MUST).** A config member that carries a
value exposes **two forms** — a raw value and a `Signal<T>`:

```
Text.make(t -> t.text("hi"))            ≡  Text.make(t -> t.text(constant("hi")))
visible(v -> v.visible(flagSignal))      // reactive visibility
frame(f -> f.width(widthSignal))         // reactive sizing, layout included
```

The **raw form is sugar for a constant signal**; a **non-constant** signal
becomes a **node-level binding** — a change re-emits only that node's `SET_TEXT`
/ `SET_PROPERTY`, and a constant emits as a plain property with **zero binding
overhead**. This holds for *every* value member, layout included
(`spacing`, `alignment`, `padding`, `frame`, `columns`, …): anything describable
in the protocol can animate. A control's two-way *value* takes a
`WritableSignal<T>`; every other member takes a one-way `Signal<T>`.

**Per-language realization.** Java cannot declare a static and an instance
method with the same signature, so the Java realization holds the values entry
**statically** (`make(...)`) and exposes the chainable forms on the returned
builder/view type — `.modifiers(...)` is an instance operation (a `View`
interface default, covariantly overridden on the builder), and static
`X.children(...)` is retained as a value-less first-call convenience. Other
languages map the operations to their idioms (extension methods, associated
functions + traits, package constructors + methods, kwargs) — see [§9.3](#93-language-adaptation-rules).

**Single-value shortcuts.** A view or modifier whose config designates a
**primary value member** MAY also expose a single-value construction overload that
is pure sugar for the config-builder lambda (views construct with `make(value)`,
modifiers with the lowercase function's value form):
---
1. **Names**: SwiftUI view/modifier names; per-language case (camelCase,
   snake_case). `foregroundStyle` not `foregroundColor`; `fontWeight`,
   `multilineTextAlignment`, `scaledToFit`, `allowsHitTesting` keep their
   SwiftUI spellings. A modifier's type is **never** suffixed `Mod`.
2. **Signature order**: canonical parameter order is preserved —
   `.border(color, width)`, `.frame(width, height, alignment)`,
   `.shadow(color, radius, x, y)`. Compound modifiers expand to one property
   per argument.
3. **Values vs modifiers**: structural/layout values and a control's bound value
   are configured through a view's `make(...)` (modifiers through lowercase
   functions); everything else is a chainable `modifiers(...)` value. The three
   operations may be chained in any order.
4. **Typed enums**: `HorizontalAlignment` (leading/center/trailing, for
   `VStack`), `VerticalAlignment` (top/center/bottom, for `HStack`), `Alignment`
   (2D — topLeading … bottomTrailing — for `ZStack`/grids and the `frame`
   modifier's content alignment); all **position-only, never stretching** (a
   child's `FILL` size kind stretches). Plus `TextAlignment`, `FontWeight`
   (100–900), `Truncation` (head/middle/tail),
   `TextCase` (none/uppercase/lowercase), `FontStyle` (normal/italic),
   `FontDesign` (default/serif/rounded/monospaced), `ContentMode` (fit/fill),
   `ControlSize` (small/regular/large), `ToggleStyle`
   (switch/checkbox/button), `PickerStyle` (menu/segmented/wheel/radiogroup),
   `DatePickerMode` (date/time/dateAndTime), `ShapeKind`
   (circle/rectangle/roundedRectangle/capsule/ellipse/path). Numeric codes
   come from MODIFIERS.md's appendix; the DSL resolves them.
5. **`Spacer`/`Color` as views**: `Spacer` is a flexible expanding filler;
   `Color` in a tree is a layout-greedy fill.
6. **The environment is the only inheritance mechanism.** Any value that must
   reach a whole subtree — a style (`ButtonStyle`), the router, the active path,
   the session's persisted state — is injected through the environment, never
   threaded through constructors and never through a second scoping system. The
   environment is a hierarchical, nearest-wins scope of typed `EnvironmentKey`
   values (the `EnvironmentBinding` modifier value / `Environment.value(key)`,
   Java; §4.5). A language MAY implement the scope with a thread-local over the
   synchronous render pass (Java does) — but that is the implementation of the
   one mechanism, not an additional one. A subtree-scoping modifier MUST be
   expressed as an `EnvironmentKey` binding: `ButtonStyle` binds
   `Environment.BUTTON_STYLE` (`EnvironmentKey<ButtonStyle>`), exactly like the
   router and the active path.
7. **Reactivity discipline**: `body()` is a tracked render; a signal read there
   subscribes the component and a later write re-renders that component, whose
   subtree is diffed into deltas. A bound node stays fine-grained (one delta, no
   body re-run). Never write signals during render. Non-signal reads are
   mount-time only ([§3.4](#34-structural-reactivity-reactive-bodies--slots)).
8. **Emission contract**: each DSL call emits exactly the documented
   properties with the documented value types; the emitter diffs. The DSL never
   computes layout, never positions, never serializes full trees.

---

## 7. Theme management

Pathland theming is **application-owned over a renderer-owned token system**
([TOKENS.md](./TOKENS.md); the wire encoding lives in [OPCODE.md](./OPCODE.md)
§Design Token System). The DSL gives the author two distinct surfaces:

# Pathland TypeScript View + Server — Implementation Plan

**Status:** Implemented (phases 1–6); phase 7 is the next follow-up
**Scope:** TypeScript-only, server-driven UI
**Last Updated:** October 22, 2026

---

## Goal

Build a TypeScript authoring and server runtime for Pathland:

- Angular-like developer experience: class views, decorators, callable signals,
  computed/effects, forced-once `body(props)`, fluent modifiers.
- The application runs on the server. The server owns the retained tree,
  signals, state, and session lifecycle.
- The browser hydrates SSR HTML and applies deltas. It does **not** run the
  view engine in this phase.
- SSR is rendered by the existing Rust `pathland-render-html` crate compiled to
  WebAssembly.
- The browser client is the existing `lib/typescript` `@pathland/dom-renderer`.
- Rust remains the source of truth for wire constants/conformance and the HTML
  renderer. Rust is not the runtime engine.

## Locked decisions

| Decision | Choice |
|---|---|
| Language | TypeScript only |
| AssemblyScript | Out of scope; no `view-as`, no closure transform, no dual-target |
| DX | Angular-like: class views, `@view`, callable signals, `body(props)`, modifiers |
| View restrictions | None from AS: optional props, closures, unions, and full TS are allowed |
| Execution model | Server-owned app; browser is a renderer |
| Browser runtime | Deferred; same TS engine must stay worker-compatible later |
| SSR | Rust `pathland-render-html` via a small wasm wrapper |
| Client | Reuse `lib/typescript` `@pathland/dom-renderer` |
| Server host | Node first; framework-agnostic core; Bun/Deno later |
| State | In-memory now; Redis interface documented and deferred |
| Context | Small `AppContext` (state/platform/route); no full Angular DI |
| Structural reactivity | Later; the reference view is static |
| Wire format | Existing 16-byte opcodes + PLPL batches, protocol v1 |

### Why not the alternatives

- **AssemblyScript / wasm app runtime:** rejected for this phase. It forces an
  AS-native DSL and a closure transform, sacrificing the Angular-like DX.
- **Rust engine runtime:** rejected. A TS app on Node would need per-call FFI;
  a non-Node host would need an embedded JS runtime. The TS engine is the future
  browser/worker runtime anyway.
- **A separate TS HTML serializer:** rejected as the primary path. Reuse the
  Rust HTML renderer for parity with the existing renderers.

## Non-goals

- No AssemblyScript compiler, transform, or runtime.
- No TS/AS byte-identity work.
- No SharedArrayBuffer ring, transferable double buffering, or worker DOM
  patcher.
- No browser-side application runtime in this phase.
- No Rust `pathland-engine` runtime dependency.
- No full Angular DI container, router, or zone.js.
- No structural/conditional rendering in phase 1; plan it as a follow-up.

---

## Architecture

```text
TypeScript view + engine (server)
        │
        ├── PLPL snapshot / delta batches
        │        ├── Rust pathland-render-html (WASM) → SSR HTML
        │        └── WebSocket → existing @pathland/dom-renderer
        │
        └── raw EVENT batches ← WebSocket ← browser
```

### Server flow

1. **SSR request**
   - Create a throwaway session with a random state scope.
   - Instantiate the app, connect state, mount the root view once.
   - Emit a full snapshot batch.
   - Render it with the Rust HTML wasm renderer.
   - Inject `data-pathland-base` and the content-hashed client bundle.
   - Close the throwaway session.
2. **WebSocket connect**
   - Client URL: `<base>/ws?wid=<window-id>`.
   - Register a pending session. The first message is `META::ENVIRONMENT`.
   - Create the live session with the `wid` state scope.
   - Do not re-send the mount frame; the client already has the SSR HTML.
3. **Deltas**
   - Signal changes emit only the affected opcodes.
   - Send monotonic PLPL batches when the connection is open.
   - `META::RESYNC` re-emits the full tree.
   - `META::PING` → `META::PONG`.
4. **Events**
   - Client sends raw EVENT batches.
   - The server updates bound signals; the engine emits deltas.
5. **Persistence**
   - Load `StateStore` values before mount.
   - Save on `State` changes.
   - Memory store now; Redis later.

## Package contracts

### `@pathland/protocol`

```text

  events.ts      # EVENT + META decode
```

```ts
export interface Opcode {
  category: number;
  command: number;
  flags: number;
  a: number;
  b: number;
  c: number;
}

export class BatchWriter {
  begin(): void;
  push(category: number, command: number, flags: number, a: number, b: number, c: number): void;
  string(value: string): number;  // arena offset
  end(sequence: number): Uint8Array;
}

export interface EventOpcode extends Opcode {
  text?: string;
}

export function decodeEvents(bytes: Uint8Array): EventOpcode[];
```

- Reuse the PLPL header/opcode/string layout already parsed by
  `lib/typescript/src/plpl.ts`.
- Use the existing implementation packing:
  `B = (valueType << 16) | propertyId`.
- F32 values are stored as raw IEEE-754 bits.
- Strings are length-prefixed UTF-8 in the batch string section.

content.text:
Don’t chase identical syntax. Define a **shared semantic vocabulary** and let each language spell it natively. That’s already the shape of `spec/DSL.md` (§9.3): same concepts, per-language realization. The recognizable parts should be the **names and semantics**, not the punctuation.

## Shared vocabulary (same everywhere)

- `View` / component render: `body()` (Java/Kotlin/TS), `build()` (Rust)
- `Signal`, `WritableSignal`, `computed`, `effect`, `untracked`
- `State`, `PersistentState`
- `ForEach` — the named reactive-list helper
- `View.of` — the named inline reactive-subtree helper
- `children`, `modifiers`, values (`make` / `new` / props)

## Per-language spellings

| Concept | Java | Kotlin | Rust | TypeScript |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Component render | `View body()` | `View body()` | `fn build(&self)` | `body(props)` |
| Signal read | `sig.get()` | `sig.value` / `sig()` | `sig.get()` | `sig()` |
| Branch | `if`/`switch` in `body()`; `View.of(() -> …)` inline | `if`/`when` expressions | `if`/`match` expressions | ternary / `switch` expressions |
| Inline subtree | `View.of(() -> …)` | `View.of { … }` (rarely needed) | `View::of(\|\| …)` | `View.of(() => …)` |
| Static list | stream/`for` + `.children(...)` | `items.map { … }` + `.children(...)` | `items.iter().map(…)` + `.children(vec![…])` | `items.map(…)` + children array |
| Reactive list | `ForEach.of(items, (item, i) -> …)` | `ForEach(items) { item, i -> … }` | `ForEach::of(items, \|item, i\| …)` | `ForEach(items, (item, i) => …)` |
| Children | `.children(a, b)` | `.children(a, b)` / trailing lambda | `.children(vec![a, b])` | `children: [a, b]` / `() => [a, b]` |
| Values | `VStack.make(v -> v.spacing(8))` | `VStack(spacing = 8)` / `make { … }` | `VStack::new(\|v\| v.spacing(8.0))` | `VStack({ spacing: 8 })` |
| Modifiers | `.modifiers(padding(16))` | `.modifiers(padding(16))` | `.modifiers(padding(16.0))` | `.modifiers(padding(16))` |

## Concrete examples

**Java**
```java
VStack.make(v -> v.spacing(8)).children(
    Text.make("Library"),
    ForEach.of(tracks, (track, index) -> TrackRowView.make(r -> r
        .track(track).index(index).trackIndex(trackIndex))));
```

**Kotlin**
```kotlin
VStack(spacing = 8) {
    Text("Library")
    ForEach(tracks) { track, index ->
        TrackRow(TrackRowProps(track, index, trackIndex))
    }
}
```
Kotlin doesn’t need `View.of` for branches — `if`/`when` are expressions:
```kotlin
VStack {
    if (showLogin.value) LoginView() else HomeView()
}
```

**Rust**
```rust
VStack::new(|v| v.spacing(8.0)).children(vec![
    Text::new("Library").into(),
    ForEach::of(tracks.clone(), |track, index| {
        TrackRow::new(track, index, track_index.clone()).into()
    }),
])
```
Branches are native expressions:
```rust
if show_login.get().unwrap_or(false) {
    LoginView::new().build()
} else {
    HomeView::new().build()
}
```

**TypeScript**
```ts
VStack({ spacing: 8 }, [
  Text({ text: "Library" }),
  ForEach(tracks, (track, index) =>
    TrackRow({ track, index, trackIndex })),
])
```
Branches are expressions:
```ts
VStack({}, [
  showLogin() ? LoginView() : HomeView(),
])
```

## Rules that keep it native and recognizable

1. **Use the language’s branch expression.** Java needs `View.of` for inline positions; Kotlin/Rust/TS do not. Don’t add a `Conditional` wrapper to languages that already have expression-level control flow.
2. **Use native iteration for static lists.** `map`/`for`/iterators are the idiomatic default. Use `ForEach` when the source is a signal or when you explicitly want a component boundary.
3. **Keep the same names for the non-native helpers**: `ForEach`, `View.of`, `Signal`, `computed`, `State`. These are the cross-language anchors.
4. **Keep `(item, index)` order** for `ForEach` to match JS `map` and Java `BiFunction`. Kotlin/Rust authors can name the lambda params; the order stays documented.
5. **Adapt construction, not semantics.** Java’s `make` builder, Kotlin’s trailing-lambda builders, Rust’s structs/`with`, and TS’s props functions are all valid spellings of the same three operations (`values`, `modifiers`, `children`).
6. **Same wire contract.** The surface differences never change emitted bytes; `ForEach`/`View.of` are still component slots with delta-only emission.

## Two current gaps to acknowledge

- The TypeScript plan on `feat/ts-dsl` is currently **static** (“no structural re-evaluation in phase 1”). It should adopt the same reactive body + `ForEach`/`View.of` semantics when structural reactivity lands.
- Rust parity is Phase 2: `build()` is still host-rebuild + diff, and `Conditional` remains until then. The cross-language contract should mark that as a parity gap, not a different semantic.

## Suggested next step

Extend `spec/DSL.md` §9.3 with **Kotlin and TypeScript columns**, plus rows for **reactive body**, **`View.of`**, and **`ForEach`**, and add the four canonical examples above. That gives each new DSL one recognizable vocabulary and one semantic contract while keeping the syntax native.

  design:
    name: Design (Style Dictionary)
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Set up Node 22
        uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: '22'
          cache: npm
          cache-dependency-path: design/package-lock.json

      # Build the generated token CSS / manifest / bundle and validate the
      # three token layers against the protocol catalog, dark/forced-dark
      # rules, and the canonical length conventions.
      - name: Install, build, check
        working-directory: design
        run: |
          npm ci
          npm run build
          npm run check

      # The Rust renderer embeds the generated bundle (committed for packaging).
      - name: Verify the committed renderer CSS matches the design build
        run: scripts/sync-design-css.sh --check

  rust:
    name: Rust (workspace + C ABI + no_std/wasm)
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    needs: [design]
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      # The workspace includes pathland-render-gtk (GTK4 + libadwaita + GStreamer)
      # and pathland-render-qt (Qt Quick), so the runner needs the GTK4,
      # libadwaita, GStreamer, and Qt system libraries before `cargo test` can
      # link them. GStreamer is required because the GTK renderer plays app-driven
      # media through a direct GStreamer playbin (GTK4's own media backend is
      # compiled out of some builds); the plugins are the runtime set the audio
      # stack uses (playbin, volume/audioconvert, mp3 decode). The Qt libraries
      # are installed in the next step.
      - name: Install GTK4 + libadwaita + GStreamer system dependencies
        run: |
          sudo apt-get update
          sudo apt-get install -y \
            libgtk-4-dev \
            libadwaita-1-dev \
            libglib2.0-dev \
            libcairo2-dev \
            libpango1.0-dev \

            libgstreamer1.0-dev \

            gstreamer1.0-plugins-good \
            gstreamer1.0-libav

      - name: Install Qt6 (QML/Quick) system dependencies
        run: |
          sudo apt-get install -y \
            qt6-base-dev \
            qt6-declarative-dev \
            qt6-declarative-private-dev \
            qt6-multimedia-dev \
            qml6-module-qtqml \
            qml6-module-qtqml-models \
            qml6-module-qtqml-workerscript \
            qml6-module-qtquick \

---
name: Release

# Publishing a GitHub Release (which creates the tag, e.g. `v0.1.1`) builds and
# publishes every artifact — the Rust crates to crates.io and the Java libraries
# to Maven Central (with the renderer's native libraries for every supported
# platform) — then attaches the built files to the Release.
#
# The tag drives the version: the workflow writes the tag's `X.Y.Z` into the Rust
# workspace version and the Java parent version (in CI only) before building, and
# a `bump` job commits that version back to `main` afterwards. No pre-bump commit
# is required. Tags must be `v<major>.<minor>.<patch>` (an optional pre-release
# suffix is allowed).
#
# The publish steps are idempotent, so re-running a partially failed release is
# safe (a crate+version already on crates.io is skipped; Maven Central rejects a
# re-deploy of an existing version).
#
# Secrets:
#   CARGO_REGISTRY_TOKEN  crates.io API token (publish scope)
#   GPG_PRIVATE_KEY       armored GPG private key (signing)
#   GPG_PASSPHRASE        its passphrase
#   CENTRAL_USERNAME      Sonatype Central Portal user token username
#   CENTRAL_PASSWORD      Sonatype Central Portal user token password

on:
  release:
    types: [published]
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      tag:
        description: 'Tag to release (e.g. v0.1.1); blank = current ref'
        required: false

permissions:
  contents: write

jobs:
  version:
    name: Resolve + validate version
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    outputs:
      tag: ${{ steps.v.outputs.tag }}
      version: ${{ steps.v.outputs.version }}
    steps:
      - id: v
        name: Derive the version from the tag
        run: |
          set -euo pipefail
          tag="${{ github.event.release.tag_name || inputs.tag || github.ref_name }}"
          if [[ ! "$tag" =~ ^v[0-9]+\.[0-9]+\.[0-9]+(-[0-9A-Za-z.-]+)?$ ]]; then
            echo "::error::tag '$tag' must be v<major>.<minor>.<patch>"
            exit 1
          fi
          version="${tag#v}"
          echo "tag=$tag version=$version"
          echo "tag=$tag" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
          echo "version=$version" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"

  rust:
    name: Publish crates to crates.io

**Recommendation: merge the reactive-body branch first, then branch from updated `main` for the DSL work.** But “merge” isn’t possible yet — the work is uncommitted, and the branch base is behind `origin/main`.

Current state:

- `feat/reactive-body-per-component` has **no commits**; all 80 files are uncommitted.
- Local `main` is **1 commit ahead** of `origin/main` (`50757889 docs(media)…`) and **2 behind** (`#167 window metadata`).
- No open PRs.
- CI runs on PRs and pushes to `main`.

## Recommended sequence

```bash
# 1. Commit the feature (single commit or code/docs split)
git add -A
git commit -m "feat(java): per-component reactive bodies (#88)"

# 2. Rebase onto the current origin/main (picks up #167)
git fetch origin
git rebase origin/main
# resolve conflicts (likely AGENTS.md + PathlandSessionTest.java), then:

# 3. Re-verify
mvn -q -f lib/java/pom.xml install
cargo test --manifest-path lib/rust/Cargo.toml
lib/rust/check-wasm.sh

# 4. Push + PR + merge
git push -u origin feat/reactive-body-per-component
gh pr create --base main --head feat/reactive-body-per-component \
  --title "feat(java): per-component reactive bodies (#88)" \
  --body "Per-component tracked bodies, View.of, Conditional removal, SizeThatFits/NavigationContainer conversion, docs/spec/status."

# 5. After merge, start DSL work from main
git checkout main
git pull --ff-only
git checkout -b feat/dsl-cross-language
```

## Why merge first

- **Every DSL depends on this model.** Swift/Kotlin/TS/Rust parity must target per-component tracking, `renderNode`, `View.of`, and the updated `spec/DSL.md`/`AGENTS.md`. Starting from `main` now means building against the old “body once / `Conditional`” contract and rebasing later.
- **Java is the reference realization.** The other DSLs need it for parity and conformance tests.
- **The spec/docs changes are the shared contract.** They should be on `main` before the DSL branches.
- **Stacking DSL work on this branch before merge is fragile.** The branch is large and still needs review/rebase; stacked branches would all need rebasing afterward.

## Two loose ends

1. **`50757889 docs(media)` is local-only.** Decide whether to include it in this PR (simplest) or push it separately first. If separate, rebase it onto `origin/main`, push, then rebase this branch on the updated main.
2. **`feat/ts-dsl` is on an older base.** After this merge, rebase it onto the new `main`; its plan says structural reactivity is deferred, so it should adopt the new `View.of`/`ForEach`/reactive-body contract.

## Commit granularity

One `feat(java): …` commit is fine for a POC. If you want reviewable history, split into:

1. core: `Emitter`, `ViewSlot`, `Signals.tracked`, `View.render/renderNode`, `PathlandNode`
2. DSL: `View.of`, remove `Conditional`, convert `NavigationContainer`/`SizeThatFits`
3. tests
4. docs/spec/status

## 9. Generation contract for a new language

An AI (or a human) generating a Pathland DSL in a new language MUST produce the
following and verify each item. This is a checklist; the authoritative details
are the companion specs.

### 9.1 Required surface

- [ ] **Views/controls** — every entry of [§4](#4-view-surface):
  `Text`, `Image`, `Color`, `Shape` (all `ShapeKind`s), `Divider`, `Spacer`,
  `ProgressView`, `Gauge`; `VStack`, `HStack`, `ZStack`, `Grid`, `GridRow`,
  `ScrollView`,
  `LazyVGrid`, `LazyHGrid`, `LazyVStack`, `LazyHStack`; `Button`,
  `TextField`, `SecureField`, `TextEditor`, `Toggle`, `Slider`, `Stepper`,
  `Picker`, `Menu`, `DatePicker`, `ColorPicker`.
- [ ] **The three operations** — configure values, apply modifiers, supply
  children — available at creation or by chaining, in any order
  ([§2](#2-canonical-signature-notation)). Each language maps them to its idiom
  ([§9.3](#93-language-adaptation-rules)).
- [ ] **Modifiers** — every entry of [§5](#5-modifier-surface), applicable to
  any view, innermost-first, emitting one property per underlying argument; a
  modifier's type carries no `Mod` suffix.
- [ ] **Custom modifiers / unified mechanism** — a `ViewModifier` authoring
  surface (`body(content) -> View`) + a chainable `modifiers(...)` operation on
  **any** view; **core modifiers are implemented through the same mechanism**,
  never a separate syntax ([§5.6](#56-custom-modifiers-developer-authored)).
- [ ] **Shared config with styles** — a style's `makeBody(Config)` receives the
  same config type the control configured via `make(...)`
  ([§5.7](#57-styleable-controls-the-style-contract)).
- [ ] **Signals** — `signal`, `computed`, `effect`, `untracked`,
  `get`/`set`/`update`/`asReadonly`, with equality suppression, synchronous
  flush, glitch-free propagation, error caching, write discipline, circular
  detection ([§3.1](#31-signal-surface)).
- [ ] **Two-way bindings** — every value control takes a writable signal (a
  config value) and exposes a sink the host routes its event into
  ([§3.2](#32-two-way-binding)).
- [ ] **Persisted state** — `State<T>` keyed fields (or the language's
  equivalent wiring) against a platform-neutral store ([§3.3](#33-persisted-state-statet)).
- [ ] **Gestures** — `.onTapGesture` (composed from raw pointer down/up) and
  raw `pointerEvents`/`EVENT_LISTENERS` bitmask ([§4.4](#44-gestures)).
- [ ] **Structural reactivity (reactive bodies)** — a signal read in a
  component body (`if`/`switch`/`for`, or the language's equivalent) re-renders
  that component and reconciles it into `TREE` deltas with zero opcodes for
  identical structure; `View.of` is the inline supplier form
  ([§3.4](#34-structural-reactivity-reactive-bodies--slots)).
- [ ] **Navigation** — `Router` / `RouteTable` / `NavigationContainer` /
  `NavigationLink` over a plain `Signal<Route>`, the initial route host-seeded
  before mount, emitting `ROUTE` and `TRANSITION` and consuming the `NAVIGATE`
  event ([§4.5](#45-navigation)).
- [ ] **Design tokens & theming** — a token surface: token-typed values usable
  in style modifiers (a `Color` accepting a token path, e.g. `Color.token("color.primary")`
  or the language's equivalent), a theme/override helper emitting
  `PARAMETER::SET_DESIGN_TOKEN` (base values + `dark.`-prefixed dark values), and
  the **base=light / `dark.*`** color-scheme convention with renderer-derived
  scheme detection — see [§7](#7-theme-management) and [TOKENS.md](./TOKENS.md).

### 9.2 Mapping rules (signature → protocol)

1. Each view/control maps to its **fixed component id** in PRIMITIVES.md.
   Application/custom component types live in `0x0100`–`0xFFFF`; a DSL must
   never reuse allocated ids.
2. Each modifier maps to the **documented property id(s)** in MODIFIERS.md
   with the documented **value type** (U8/U32/I32/F32/STRING/ENUM/COLOR/
   DESIGN_TOKEN). Enumerated values use the numeric codes in MODIFIERS.md's
   appendix.
3. `Color` values pack as sRGB `0xAARRGGBB`. A **token-typed** value instead
   carries the `DESIGN_TOKEN` value type with the token path in the arena
   (never a packed literal); the renderer resolves it against the current
   scheme. A theme/override helper emits `PARAMETER::SET_DESIGN_TOKEN`
   (`A` = arenaRef path, `B` = valueType, `C` = value); a `dark.`-prefixed path
   supplies the dark design (base = light — [TOKENS.md](./TOKENS.md)).
4. `WIDTH`/`HEIGHT` sentinels: `FILL` = −1.0, `HUG_CONTENT` = −2.0.
5. `Grid` counts map to the **config values** `GRID_COLUMNS` (`0x001E`) /
   `GRID_ROWS` (`0x001F`): a positive `int` count emits a positive F32; absent =
   auto-fit. A **`List<GridItem>`** value serializes to the **`GRID_TRACKS`**
   (`0x0020`, STRING) per-track spec, which takes precedence over the counts. A
   `WIDTH`/`HEIGHT` frame on a grid is the grid's **box**, never a count
   ([§4.2](#42-layout--container-nodes)).
6. `DatePicker` value/event use the two-field encoding **days since epoch
   (I32) + millis of day (U32)**; there is no `DATE_VALUE` property.
7. Value/text/date events are gated by the transport-aware event guards; the
   DSL's controls emit the `ACTION_ID`/`BINDING_ID`/`EVENT_LISTENERS` that
   declare intent.
8. Emission is **diff-based and reactive**: the DSL describes values, the
   emitter diffs. A generated DSL must keep the retained tree + emitter
   separation; it must not hand-serialize full trees.

### 9.3 Language adaptation rules

**The three operations are normative; their spellings are not.** A conformant
DSL MUST expose *configure values*, *apply modifiers*, and *supply children*,
each available at creation or by chaining (any order), mapped to the host
language's idioms. The canonical (SwiftUI-shaped) spelling is
`Text("x").padding(16)`; Java spells values `make(...)` (views) / lowercase
functions (modifiers) and chains `modifiers(...)` / `children(...)`.

| Aspect | Java | C# | Rust | Go | Python |
|--------|------|----|------|----|--------|
| configure values | `make(c -> …)` (views) / `padding(c -> …)` (modifiers) | `Make(c => …)` | `Type::new(config)` / `with(\|c\| …)` | ctor + options | kwargs / `configure(…)` |
| single-value shortcut | `make(value)` / `padding(value)` (sugar for the lambda) | `Make(value)` | `Type::new(value)` / `Type(sig)` | `Type(val)` | `Type(val=…)` / `Type(sig)` |
| apply modifiers | `.modifiers(…)` | `.Modifiers(…)` | `.modifiers(…)` (single or tuple) | `.Modifiers(…)` | `.modifiers(…)` |
| supply children | `.children(…)` | `.Children(…)` | `.children(vec![…])` / `vstack![…]` | ctor args / `.Children(…)` | `.children(*v)` |
| creation + chaining | static on the view; chain on the returned builder | static on the view; chain via **extension methods** | associated fn `Type::new`; chain via a **trait** + macros | package ctor; chain via methods | kwargs + methods |

Here’s the plan I’d execute after approval. It adds the cross-language vocabulary, the missing Java list primitive, and commits the result.

## 1. Java DSL: add `ForEach`

New `ForEach` component (the missing Java piece alongside `View.of`):

```java
public final class ForEach {
    // static list: maps once per render
    public static <T> View of(List<T> items, BiFunction<T, Integer, View> content);

    // reactive list: the component's tracked render reads the signal
    public static <T> View of(Signal<List<T>> items, BiFunction<T, Integer, View> content);
}
```

- Group-backed component (same shape as `View.of`); each item is a child component slot.
- Null children are skipped; callback order is `(item, index)`.
- Static list maps per render; `Signal<List<T>>` re-renders only the `ForEach` slot.
- No keys: the emitter still diffs by position + type; document that.
- Optional wrapper-free `ForEach.views(...)` for static lists (returns `View[]`), if you want it.

Tests (`ForEachTest`): static order, signal add/remove, identical recompute → zero opcodes, null skip, nested `ForEach`, bound signals inside rows, environment scope.

## 2. Cross-language vocabulary

Add a new **`spec/DSL.md` §9.3.1 “Cross-language reactive vocabulary”**:

- Table columns: **Swift, Java, Kotlin, Rust, TypeScript**.
- Rows: component render, signal read, branch, inline subtree, static list, reactive list, children, values, modifiers, state, environment.
- Canonical examples for all five languages (the ones we discussed).
- Rules:
  - Native control flow where the language has it; `View.of` only where needed (Java inline).
  - Native iteration for static lists; `ForEach` for reactive/component-scoped lists.
  - Same names for the non-native anchors: `ForEach`, `View.of`, `Signal`, `computed`, `State`.
  - `(item, index)` order.
  - Gaps: Rust parity Phase 2; TS structural reactivity deferred; Kotlin/Swift not implemented.

Also update:

- `spec/DSL.md` §3.4 table: Java column gets `ForEach.of(signal, …)` for reactive lists.
- `spec/DSL.md` §9.1 required surface: add `ForEach`.
- `AGENTS.md`: short pointer to §9.3.1 and a `ForEach` mention.
- `lib/java/pathland-view/status.md`: `ForEach` implemented + tests.

## 3. Verify

```bash
mvn -q -f lib/java/pom.xml install
cargo test --manifest-path lib/rust/Cargo.toml
lib/rust/check-wasm.sh
git diff --check
```

## 4. Commit

Recommended two commits on `feat/reactive-body-per-component`:

# Plan: common vocabulary + Java `ForEach` + two commits

## 1. Commit the existing reactive-body work first

Before adding anything, verify and commit the current branch state as commit 1.

```bash
mvn -q -f lib/java/pom.xml install
cargo test --manifest-path lib/rust/Cargo.toml
lib/rust/check-wasm.sh
git diff --check

git add -A
git commit -m "feat(java): per-component reactive bodies (#88)"
```

This isolates the core change (tracked bodies, `renderNode`, `View.of`, `Conditional` removal, `NavigationContainer`/`SizeThatFits`, tests, spec/AGENTS/status).

## 2. Add the Java `ForEach` component

New `lib/java/pathland-view/src/main/java/dev/pathland/view/ForEach.java`:

```java
public final class ForEach {
    // static list: maps once per render
    public static <T> View of(List<T> items, BiFunction<T, Integer, View> content);

    // reactive list: the component's tracked render reads the signal
    public static <T> View of(Signal<List<T>> items, BiFunction<T, Integer, View> content);
}
```

Implementation (`ForEachView<T>`, package-private):

```java
@Override
public PathlandNode renderNode(Environment env) {
    PathlandNode node = new PathlandNode(Components.VSTACK); // Group-backed slot
    List<T> list = source.get(); // tracked for the Signal overload
    if (list != null) {
        for (int i = 0; i < list.size(); i++) {
            View child = content.apply(list.get(i), i);
            if (child != null) {
                node.children.add(child.render(env));
            }
        }
    }
    return node;
}
```

- `(item, index)` callback order.
- Null children skipped; null source treated as empty.
- Static overload maps per render; `Signal<List<T>>` re-renders only the `ForEach` slot.
- Group wrapper documented; diff is position + type (no keys).
- No `when`/`Case` re-add — bare `if`/`switch` + `View.of` remain the Java branch spelling.

Add `ForEachTest`:

1. Static list renders in order.
2. Signal list add/remove emits `TREE` deltas only.
3. Identical recompute emits zero opcodes.
4. Null children skipped.
5. Nested `ForEach`.
6. Bound signal inside a row stays fine-grained.
7. Environment scope reaches rows.

Leave `LibraryView` on its static stream (the form you liked); `ForEach` is the reactive/list-scoped component.

## 3. Add the cross-language vocabulary

New **`spec/DSL.md` §9.3.1 “Cross-language reactive vocabulary”**:

| Concept | Swift | Java | Kotlin | Rust | TypeScript |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Component | `var body: some View` | `View body()` | `View body()` | `fn build(&self)` | `body(props)` |
| Signal read | `count` / `signal.value` | `sig.get()` | `sig.value` / `sig()` | `sig.get()` | `sig()` |
| Branch | `if`/`switch` in `@ViewBuilder` | `if`/`switch` in `body()`; `View.of` inline | `if`/`when` expressions | `if`/`match` | ternary / `switch` |
| Inline subtree | `Group { … }` | `View.of(() -> …)` | `View.of { … }` | `View::of(\|\| …)` | `View.of(() => …)` |
| Static list | `ForEach(items)` / `for` | stream/`for` + `.children` | `items.map { … }` | iterator + `.children(vec![…])` | `items.map(…)` |
| Reactive list | `ForEach(items) { … }` | `ForEach.of(items, (item, i) -> …)` | `ForEach(items) { item, i -> … }` | `ForEach::of(items, \|item, i\| …)` | `ForEach(items, (item, i) => …)` |
| Children | trailing closure | `.children(a, b)` | `.children(a, b)` | `.children(vec![a, b])` | `children: [a, b]` |
| Values | `VStack(spacing: 8)` | `VStack.make(v -> v.spacing(8))` | `VStack(spacing = 8)` | `VStack::new(\|v\| v.spacing(8.0))` | `VStack({ spacing: 8 })` |
| Modifiers | `.padding(16)` | `.modifiers(padding(16))` | `.modifiers(padding(16))` | `.modifiers(padding(16.0))` | `.modifiers(padding(16))` |
| State | `@State` / `@Binding` | `State<T>` / `WritableSignal<T>` | same as Java | same as Java | same as Java |
| Environment | `@Environment` | `Environment.value(key)` | same as Java | `Environment` | `useAppContext()` |

- Use native control flow where the language has it; `View.of` only where needed (Java inline).

### 9.3 Language adaptation rules

**The three operations are normative; their spellings are not.** A conformant
DSL MUST expose *configure values*, *apply modifiers*, and *supply children*,
each available at creation or by chaining (any order), mapped to the host
language's idioms. The canonical (SwiftUI-shaped) spelling is
`Text("x").padding(16)`; Java spells values `make(...)` (views) / lowercase
functions (modifiers) and chains `modifiers(...)` / `children(...)`.

| Aspect | Java | C# | Rust | Go | Python |
|--------|------|----|------|----|--------|
| configure values | `make(c -> …)` (views) / `padding(c -> …)` (modifiers) | `Make(c => …)` | `Type::new(config)` / `with(\|c\| …)` | ctor + options | kwargs / `configure(…)` |
| single-value shortcut | `make(value)` / `padding(value)` (sugar for the lambda) | `Make(value)` | `Type::new(value)` / `Type(sig)` | `Type(val)` | `Type(val=…)` / `Type(sig)` |
| apply modifiers | `.modifiers(…)` | `.Modifiers(…)` | `.modifiers(…)` (single or tuple) | `.Modifiers(…)` | `.modifiers(…)` |
| supply children | `.children(…)` | `.Children(…)` | `.children(vec![…])` / `vstack![…]` | ctor args / `.Children(…)` | `.children(*v)` |
| creation + chaining | static on the view; chain on the returned builder | static on the view; chain via **extension methods** | associated fn `Type::new`; chain via a **trait** + macros | package ctor; chain via methods | kwargs + methods |
| same-name static + chain | **builder split** (static on class, chain on builder) | extension methods (separate static class) | assoc fn + trait method | package func + method (not type-scoped) | **not expressible** (methods are last-wins) |
| `with` name legal | yes | yes (`With`; lowercase `with` is the record keyword) | yes | yes | **no** — `with` is a keyword → kwargs / `configure` |
| varargs children | yes | `params` | no — slices/arrays or macros | `...` | `*args` |
| value *is* the modifier | enum OK | **enum can't implement an interface** → `record struct` / static readonly value | enum OK | typed const + method OK | enum member with `apply` OK |

Rules:

- A language that cannot express "static-or-chained under one name" (Python)
  MUST still offer the three operations — value configuration via kwargs /
  `configure(...)`, modifiers and children via chainable methods.
- A language whose enums cannot implement the modifier interface (C#) MUST
  supply the equivalent single-value modifier form (a `record struct`, a static
  readonly value, or an implicit conversion).
- **Reactive values are config members, in every language.** A config member
  accepts a raw value or a signal ([§2](#2-canonical-signature-notation)). Rust
  realizes this with `impl Into<Reactive<T>>` on each builder setter
  (`Reactive<T> { Static(T), Signal(SignalId) }`); the former `Bound` /
  `*.bound` modifier surface is folded into it and **removed**.
- Names are recommendations; semantics
  ([§1](#1-design-principles-dsl-flavored)) are the contract.

### 9.4 Conformance recipe

A generated DSL is verified by proving it **emits the same bytes** as the
reference implementations:

  now works in `body()` (bare control flow), with `View.of(Supplier<View>)` as the
  inline supplier form. The root chain (`body()` delegation, modifiers,
  environment/tap/navigation wrappers) stays in one slot; child views are child
  slots. A bound signal (`Text.make(t -> t.text(signal))`) remains fine-grained and
  does not re-run the body (initial binding reads are untracked). Non-signal reads
